title: GiveDirectly paid anticipatory cash in Kogi State, Nigeria, on Google Flood Hub forecast triggers (August to October 2024)
summary: Google Flood Hub forecast triggers paid $105 to 4,600 people in Ibaji, Kogi State, mostly before floods peaked on 21 October 2024
account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts by application programming interface (API), made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. When 20% of a community's area was forecast to flood the trigger was met and verified residents were paid. The New Humanitarian describes an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. 3,250 were paid between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. Its own survey reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. A New Humanitarian investigation (31 August 2026) found data mismatches and phone-access barriers excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation appeared.
purpose: Trigger and target anticipatory cash transfers to flood-prone communities before river flooding.
system: Google Flood Hub AI river-flood forecasts accessed via API, with JBA Global Resilience hydrology analysis and a 20%-of-community-area trigger rule
developer: Google (Flood Hub); trigger design by GiveDirectly with JBA Global Resilience
domain: Humanitarian anticipatory action and cash transfers
taxonomy_note: Cash paid before a forecast flood is read as reducing potential for harm; Trustible's description stresses legal harm.

ratings.reason: $105 to over 4,600 individuals, followed by a $210 transfer (recipient count not stated). Implementer survey reports weekly income doubling and fewer food shortages (self-reported, not independently verified).

GiveDirectly gained a tested trigger pipeline and documented lessons. It acknowledged to The New Humanitarian that it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation was published on 31 August 2026.
Material to a group of about 4,600 people in 53 communities. The investigation documents that some of the poorest were excluded, limiting wider benefit.

ai_role.statement: Decisive for timing and geography: GiveDirectly told The New Humanitarian that satellite/AI flood modeling determined which communities were paid and when. Individual eligibility was decided by non-AI verification (ward residence, Smile ID checks, call-center calls). The investigation identifies that as the main source of exclusions. GiveDirectly's own page attributes the late payments to identity checks in two wards.

fields.account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts by application programming interface (API), made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. When 20% of a community's area was forecast to flood the trigger was met and verified residents were paid. The New Humanitarian describes an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. 3,250 were paid between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. Its own survey reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. A New Humanitarian investigation (31 August 2026) found data mismatches and phone-access barriers excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation appeared.

fields.account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts by application programming interface (API), made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. When 20% of a community's area was forecast to flood the trigger was met and verified residents were paid. The New Humanitarian describes an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. 3,250 were paid between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. Its own survey reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. A New Humanitarian investigation (31 August 2026) found data mismatches and phone-access barriers excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation appeared.

echoes.setting: GiveDirectly's 2022 Kogi State response: communities chosen before the season by layering historical flood data (Floodbase, Fathom), granular poverty maps and crop and village density derived from satellite imagery; people enrolled mid-September 2022 and paid once October 2022 flooding began (month only known; first day used)
GiveDirectly anticipatory programs in Kenya, Mozambique and a planned Bangladesh RCT (Jamuna basin)

display.answer: GiveDirectly and JBA used Flood Hub forecasts to identify communities where at least 20% of the area was expected to flood. GiveDirectly verified residents’ identities and bank details before sending payments.
